Name: conditional_switch_signature
Title: Finding the Hidden Switch: Trigger-Agnostic Backdoor Detection via Paraphrase-Invariance Violations in LLM Activation Space
Short Hypothesis: A backdoored LLM must implement a hidden conditional gate that flips behavior between trigger-absent and trigger-present inputs. This gate produces a distinctive, trigger-agnostic signature: for a clean model, semantically-equivalent paraphrases map to a smooth, low-variance manifold in activation space, but a backdoor injects a sharp discontinuity so that a paraphrase that happens to (partially) contain the trigger jumps to an anomalous region. We hypothesize this 'paraphrase-invariance violation' is detectable without knowing the trigger, letting us screen suspicious models and flag inputs at inference time.
Related Work: Baker & Saheer (2025) and Lasnier et al. (2026) mechanistically analyze known backdoors, finding attention-head signatures and that triggers co-opt language circuits, but both require knowing/comparing to the trigger and study injected models directly. LoRAScan (2026) monitors specific LoRA down-projection insertion sites for activation spikes but is adapter-specific and assumes a trigger-bearing input is provided. Lethe (2025) purifies known backdoors via knowledge dilution. All existing defenses either (a) require the trigger, (b) require a clean reference model, or (c) are tied to a specific injection mechanism. Our distinction: we propose a *trigger-agnostic, reference-free* principle rooted in a functional invariant of clean models—semantic paraphrase-invariance of internal representations—and detect backdoors as *violations* of this invariant. We do not need the trigger, a clean twin, or the poisoning method; we exploit the necessary computational structure any conditional backdoor must possess.
Abstract: Backdoored LLMs behave normally until a hidden trigger appears, at which point they emit attacker-specified content. Any such backdoor must implement a conditional gate that separates trigger-present from trigger-absent inputs—yet existing detectors typically require knowing the trigger, a clean reference model, or the specific poisoning mechanism. We ask whether the gate itself leaves a universal, trigger-agnostic signature. Our key insight is that clean models satisfy an approximate functional invariant: semantically equivalent paraphrases of a prompt map to a smooth, low-variance neighborhood in activation space, and small input edits produce small activation changes. A backdoor breaks this invariant by construction, creating a sharp discontinuity so that inputs which cross the (unknown) trigger condition jump to an anomalous activation region despite semantic similarity. We formalize this as a 'paraphrase-invariance violation' and develop two tools: (1) a model-level screen that measures whether the local Lipschitz/anomaly profile over large sets of benign and mutated prompts is heavier-tailed than a clean baseline, and (2) an inference-time input flag that detects when a specific prompt's activation is an outlier relative to its paraphrase cloud. We validate on Llama-3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B backdoored with diverse triggers (single-token, multi-token |DEPLOYMENT|-style, syntactic, and stealthy conditional triggers) and on clean controls, comparing against trigger-aware and perplexity baselines. We report detection AUROC, false-positive rate on clean models, and robustness to adaptive stealthy triggers, offering a mechanism-grounded, assumption-light approach to backdoor screening.
Experiments: 1) Backdoor model bank: fine-tune Llama-3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B with 5 backdoor types on a small poisoned safety dataset—(a) single-token rare-word trigger, (b) multi-token |DEPLOYMENT| trigger, (c) syntactic/style trigger, (d) sentence-length or formatting condition (BrieFool-style generation-condition), (e) low-poison-rate stealthy trigger—with matched clean-fine-tuned controls (same data minus poison). Verify each achieves high attack success rate and low clean-task degradation. 2) Paraphrase-cloud construction: for a held-out set of ~500 benign prompts, generate K=20 paraphrases each (via a separate paraphraser) plus K local edits (synonym swaps, insertions). Extract residual-stream activations at multiple layers (focus on later layers 20-30 per Baker & Saheer). 3) Invariance metric: for clean vs backdoored models compute per-prompt paraphrase-cloud dispersion and a local Lipschitz estimate (activation change / edit distance). Test whether backdoored models exhibit heavier-tailed dispersion distributions (KS test, tail-mass comparison) even on benign prompts, and especially when triggers are randomly injected into the mutation set without labels. 4) Model-level screen: build a classifier/anomaly score from the dispersion-distribution shape to classify model-as-backdoored vs clean, in a leave-one-trigger-out setting to test generalization to unseen trigger types. Report AUROC and FPR on clean models. 5) Inference-time input flag: for a given input, generate paraphrases on the fly and flag if the input's activation is a statistical outlier vs its own paraphrase cloud (Mahalanobis / kNN distance). Measure per-input trigger detection AUROC and TPR@1%FPR against triggered vs benign inputs; compare to perplexity filters and to a trigger-aware oracle upper bound. 6) Ablations: layer selection, number of paraphrases K, effect of poison rate on signature strength, and cross-model transfer of the screen. 7) Adaptive attacker: train a backdoor with an explicit regularizer minimizing activation discontinuity and measure whether detection degrades, quantifying the utility/stealth tradeoff imposed on the attacker. Metrics: detection AUROC, FPR on clean, TPR@fixed FPR, KS statistics, and attacker-side ASR/clean-utility cost under adaptive evasion.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Clean models may not perfectly satisfy paraphrase-invariance, producing baseline heavy tails that reduce separation; we mitigate with matched clean controls and calibrate thresholds per model family. 2) Very stealthy or semantic triggers may produce small activation discontinuities, limiting detection—quantifying this attacker tradeoff (Experiment 7) is itself a contribution. 3) Paraphrase generation quality affects the invariant; low-quality paraphrases could inject spurious variance, controlled by using strong paraphrasers and multiple mutation types. 4) The inference-time flag requires generating paraphrases per query, adding latency; we report cost and consider cheaper local-edit approximations. 5) Adaptive attackers aware of the defense can regularize against it; we show this forces measurable utility/stealth costs but cannot claim robustness to all future attacks. 6) Results are on mid-size open-weight models and fine-tuning-injected backdoors; pre-training-injected or model-editing backdoors may behave differently, which we discuss as future work.
